title: Brunei and the Philippines
hookLine: Muslim sultanates of Borneo and Mindanao

cards: A street sign in Brunei, on the island of Borneo. The road's name is written twice: once in Latin letters, the way Malay is usually written today, and once above it in flowing Arabic letters.
Same words, same language, two alphabets. That second script, Jawi, is Malay written in the letters of the Qur'an, a small daily clue to a bigger story.
North and east of Borneo, across the sea, on the southern islands of the Philippines, there are clues like it. Today: Brunei and the Philippines.

teach.h: TRADE WINDS TO BORNEO AND THE ISLANDS.
teach.b: The trade winds that carried merchants to Malacca also carried them along the coasts of Borneo and up into the southern Philippine islands. Where trading towns took up Islam, local rulers often took a new title: sultan.
On Borneo, the Sultanate of Brunei grew into a sea power along the coast.
It's still ruled by a sultan today, with Islam at the heart of public life and Jawi on its signs.
Further north, on the islands of Sulu and Mindanao, the Sultanates of Sulu and Maguindanao rose and ruled the seas and rivers around them.
Their Muslim peoples, the Tausug, the Maguindanao, the Maranao and others, are often called together the Moro.
When Spain later took the northern islands, the southern sultanates resisted, and that history of struggle over land and self-rule runs long and hard, into modern times.
Today much of the Muslim south forms the Bangsamoro autonomous region, within the Philippines. And there are stories.

Around Lake Lanao, the Maranao keep the Darangen, a long epic sung by performers, full of heroes, journeys, love and the old kingdom of Bembaran, sung at weddings and gatherings to hold up a people's memory of who they are.

teach.h: THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.
teach.b: The Qur'an says: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Sultans, seas, an epic by a lake. The sultanates of the islands.

how: In Brunei, Islam shapes public life and Malay is written in both Latin letters and Jawi; Muslims of the southern Philippines keep their own languages, sung epics such as the Darangen, and traditions from the old sultanates.

games.q: you're walking in Brunei. a street sign shows the road's name in Latin letters, and again above it in another script. which script is it?
games.why: Jawi: the same Malay words, written in the letters of the Qur'an, a daily clue to how Islam came to the islands.

practice: An epic is a people remembering out loud.

Run one story your family or town keeps telling through your mind, slowly, the way a singer would: a journey, a hero, a loss, a wedding that went wrong, and hold it beside the Darangen, sung by a lake far away.
If you pray, you can ask for the good of the people of those islands.

wordCard.voice: Moro. The Muslim peoples of Sulu and Mindanao, including the Tausug, Maguindanao and Maranao, under sultanates where Islam came by sea. Today's word.
